title: The Chernobyl disaster (1986)
subtitle: April 26, 1986
subject: sciences
description: On April 26, 1986, reactor No. 4 at Chernobyl exploded. It is the worst civil nuclear accident in history. Here is what happened, without the sensationalism.

hero.hook: One night in April 1986, a safety test turned into a disaster. All of Europe would live with the fallout.

blocks.text: On **April 26, 1986**, at 1:23 in the morning, reactor No. 4 of the **Chernobyl** power plant, then in Soviet Ukraine, became the scene of the worst known civil nuclear accident. On the [[INES]] scale, which rates nuclear events from 1 to 7, it reached the top level, like Fukushima in 2011.

Radioactive material was thrown into the atmosphere. The cloud crossed much of Europe. Beyond the human tragedy, Chernobyl changed the way people saw nuclear power for good, and it exposed the flaws of the Soviet system.

It all started with a safety test. The engineers wanted to check whether, in a power cut, the still-spinning turbines could run the cooling pumps until the diesel generators started. The idea was sound. The conditions of the test were not.

blocks.caption: The containment dome over reactor No. 4, ringed by the abandoned buildings of Pripyat

blocks.text: The night shift was working at low power. But the [[Soviet RBMK reactor]], a design cooled by water and moderated by graphite, turns very unstable in that state. In this type of reactor, steam bubbles can speed the reaction up instead of slowing it down.

When the operator hit the emergency shutdown, the control rods meant to stop the reaction first caused a brief surge, because of the way they were built. The power ran away. Steam blew the core apart. The protective slab, weighing about **1,000 tons**, was thrown aside. The reactor lay open to the sky.
Down in the basement, a nuclear lava nicknamed the “Elephant's Foot” had formed. In 1986, staying near it for too long meant death within days.

In the first hours, many people thought it was just a roof fire. Firefighters went in without proper protection. Some handled radioactive graphite without knowing it. The symptoms of acute radiation sickness came quickly: nausea, burns.

The nearby town of **Pripyat**, built for the plant's workers, carried on as normal for about **36 hours**. Children played outside. Only on **April 27** were its **50,000** residents evacuated, in a matter of hours, often with almost nothing.

To contain the disaster, the USSR mobilized nearly **600,000** people: the [[liquidators]]. Helicopter pilots, workers, soldiers. Some had only a few dozen seconds on the roof to clear debris, because the remote-controlled robots broke down under the radiation.
Some liquidators received a medal showing a drop of blood crossed by rays. A rare decoration, created for an invisible danger.

The cloud left radioactive iodine and cesium over huge areas. The WHO recognizes about **4,000** cases of thyroid cancer, mostly in children exposed through contaminated milk. The total long-term death toll is still debated from one study to the next.

Around the site, a [[30 km exclusion zone]] was evacuated. Forty years later, with no farming and no towns, wildlife there is often abundant: wolves, moose, Przewalski's horses. Radioactivity is still a danger, but the absence of people has, paradoxically, left room for nature.

In 1986, a first concrete sarcophagus sealed off the reactor. As it weakened, it was covered in **2016** by a huge steel arch, the New Safe Confinement, built to last about **100 years** and assembled away from the site, then slid into place to limit the workers' exposure.

For [[Mikhail Gorbachev]], then the leader of the USSR, Chernobyl laid bare bureaucratic secrecy and industrial negligence. The accident pushed the country toward more openness, known as glasnost, and sped up the crisis of the Soviet regime.

Around the world, the idea of nuclear power without serious risk was shaken. In **1989**, operators created [[WANO]], the World Association of Nuclear Operators, to share good safety practice between countries. Several states slowed or rethought their programs.
Chernobyl (1986) remains the symbol of a major nuclear accident: a design flaw, human error, and secrecy. The exclusion zone is still empty, while nuclear safety worldwide had to reinvent itself.
